html-b01-what-is-html.q: A colleague claims a web page needs no programming at all to exist. For a page of pure text content, are they right?
options: No — every page needs at least some JavaScript to render
Yes — HTML alone describes the content, and the browser renders it without any programming
No — HTML must be compiled into a program before browsers can open it
Only if the server converts the HTML into images first
html-b01-what-is-html.why: HTML is a markup language: it labels content, and the browser parses and renders it directly. No code execution, compiling or scripting is required for a content page.

html-b01-what-is-html.q: You type a site's address and press Enter. What is the first thing your browser receives back for the page?
options: A rendered screenshot of the page
The page's CSS styling rules
The HTML document as plain text
A compiled binary of the page
html-b01-what-is-html.why: The server's response to the initial request is the HTML text itself; the browser then parses it and may issue further requests for images, styles and scripts.

html-b01-what-is-html.q: You write <heding>Welcome</heding> by mistake. What will the browser do?
options: Show an error message explaining the typo
Refuse to render the rest of the page
Automatically correct it to <h1>
Render the text without any heading meaning or styling, reporting nothing
html-b01-what-is-html.why: Browsers ignore unknown tags silently — the text still appears, but no heading semantics or default styling apply, and no error is ever shown.

html-b02-editors-setup.q: You edited index.html in VS Code, switched to the browser, refreshed — and the change is not there. What is the most likely cause?
options: The file was never saved after editing
HTML files need to be recompiled after each change
The browser cache must be deleted every time
VS Code cannot edit files that a browser has open
html-b02-editors-setup.why: The browser reads the file from disk, and unsaved changes exist only in the editor's memory. Save first, then refresh — it is the most common beginner stumble.

html-b02-editors-setup.q: You want to see the exact HTML text a live website's server sent, unmodified. Which tool shows that?
options: The DevTools Elements panel
View page source
The browser's reading mode
The downloads list
html-b02-editors-setup.why: View-source shows the raw document as sent. The DevTools Elements panel shows the live DOM after parsing, repairs and script changes — related, but not the same text.

html-b02-editors-setup.q: A friend wrote their first page in Microsoft Word and saved it as page.html from Word's save dialog. The browser shows garbled clutter. Why?
options: Word documents are too large for browsers to open
The page is missing a doctype declaration
Word saves formatting data around the text, so the file is not the plain-text HTML the browser expects
Browsers block files created by word processors for security
html-b02-editors-setup.why: HTML must be plain text. Word processors embed their own formatting markup, so the saved file contains far more than the typed tags — use a code editor or plain-text editor instead.

html-b03-document-anatomy.q: A layout renders with strangely computed widths, and you notice the file's first line is a comment, with <!DOCTYPE html> on line two. What is going on?
options: Comments are invalid in HTML files
The doctype only works when written in lowercase
Content before the doctype can push browsers into quirks mode, changing how CSS behaves
The html element is missing a lang attribute
html-b03-document-anatomy.why: The doctype must be the very first thing in the file; anything before it risks quirks mode, where box sizing and other CSS behaviours imitate legacy browsers.

html-b03-document-anatomy.q: You are building a page whose content is written in Greek. Which markup declares that correctly?
options: <html lang="el">
<html language="greek">
<body lang="gr">
<meta charset="el">
html-b03-document-anatomy.why: The lang attribute belongs on the html root element and takes a standard language code — el for Greek. charset declares text encoding, not language.

html-b03-document-anatomy.q: Where must the <title> element live, and what happens if you leave it out?
options: In the body; without it the h1 disappears
In the head; without it the tab shows the file name or URL and search results suffer
Anywhere; browsers relocate it automatically with no downside
Before the doctype, or browsers use quirks mode
html-b03-document-anatomy.why: title is head-only metadata naming the document for tabs, bookmarks and search results. Omitting it leaves the browser falling back to the file name or URL.

html-b04-elements-nesting.q: Which of these lines is correctly nested?
options: launch day
launch day
launch day
launch day
html-b04-elements-nesting.why: The most recently opened element must close first — em opened last, so it closes before strong. Crossed tags force the browser to guess a repair.

html-b04-elements-nesting.q: A teammate writes and asks if the closing tag is required. What do you tell them?
options: Yes — every element needs a closing tag
img is a void element: it has no closing tag at all, so </img> should be removed
Only needed when the image has an alt attribute
It is required in HTML5 but optional in older HTML
html-b04-elements-nesting.why: img is one of the void elements (br, hr, img, input, meta, link...). They consist of a single tag; closing tags for them are invalid and discarded by the parser.

html-b04-elements-nesting.q: In a plain HTML file you write <div/> expecting a self-closed empty div. What does the parser actually do?
options: Creates an empty, properly closed div
Ignores the slash and treats it as an ordinary opening <div> that still needs closing
Reports a syntax error in the console
Converts the div into a void element
html-b04-elements-nesting.why: In HTML5 the trailing slash is meaningless. On void elements it is harmlessly ignored; on normal elements like div it still leaves the element open — a classic source of broken layouts.

html-b05-attributes.q: An image file is named team photo.jpg. Which markup loads it reliably?
html-b05-attributes.why: Quotes keep the space inside the value. Unquoted, the parser cuts the value at the space and mangles the rest — which is why professionals quote every attribute value.

html-b05-attributes.q: You render <input type="checkbox" checked="false"> and the box appears ticked. Why?
options: The value false is misspelled — it needs to be False
checked is a boolean attribute: its presence means on, and the value is ignored entirely
Checkboxes are always ticked by default in every browser
The type attribute overrides the checked attribute
html-b05-attributes.why: For boolean attributes like checked, disabled and required, existence is the whole signal — even checked="false" means checked. The only off switch is removing the attribute.

html-b05-attributes.q: You need to style a specific paragraph uniquely and also mark it as one of many 'note' paragraphs. Which combination is right?
options: — two ids cover both needs
— classes replace ids entirely
— a unique id plus a shared class
— the name attribute handles both
html-b05-attributes.why: id values are unique per page (one element, one id), while classes are reusable labels many elements can share — and one element can carry both attributes at once.

html-b06-headings.q: A blog post page has the post title, three section titles, and one sub-point under the second section. Which outline is correct?
options: h1 for the title, h2 for each section, h3 for the sub-point
h1 for everything, sized differently with CSS
h1 for the title, h3 for sections because they look better, h4 for the sub-point
h2 for the title and h1 for sections to emphasise content
html-b06-headings.why: One h1 describes the page, major sections take h2, and subsections nest one level deeper — never skipping levels downwards.

html-b06-headings.q: A designer wants a small-looking heading and suggests using h5 for a major section since it renders smaller. What is the right response?
options: Agree — heading tags exist to control text size
Use h2 for the structure and change its size with CSS — levels encode outline, not appearance
Use a bold paragraph instead of any heading
Use h5 but add extra bold styling to compensate
html-b06-headings.why: Heading levels are structural. Screen readers and search engines read the level, not the font size — appearance is CSS's job.

html-b06-headings.q: Why do screen-reader users particularly benefit from a correct heading structure?
options: Headings are read in a louder voice
They can jump directly between headings to navigate, hearing each level announced
Screen readers skip all non-heading text automatically
Headings load faster than paragraphs
html-b06-headings.why: Heading navigation is a core screen-reader feature: users skim a page by jumping heading to heading, so skipped levels and fake bold-text headings genuinely break navigation.

html-b07-paragraphs.q: In your source file you separate two paragraphs of text with three blank lines but no tags. How does the browser render them?
options: As two paragraphs with a large gap
As one continuous block — the blank lines collapse to a single space
As two paragraphs with a small gap
It depends on the browser's default font
html-b07-paragraphs.why: All runs of whitespace, including line breaks, collapse to one space in normal HTML text. Only p elements create paragraph blocks.

html-b07-paragraphs.q:
You need vertical space between a heading and the text below it, and a teammate suggests

. What is the professional approach?
options:
Use

— that is what br is for

Use empty

elements instead
Use CSS margin for spacing; br is only for breaks that are part of the text's meaning, like poem lines
Use an hr styled to be invisible
html-b07-paragraphs.why: br belongs to content whose line breaks carry meaning (poems, addresses). Visual spacing between blocks is presentation, which CSS margin handles responsively.

html-b07-paragraphs.q: You want to display a small text-based table where columns align using spaces. Which element preserves your spacing exactly?
options: with extra spaces typed in
<blockquote>
<pre>
<mark>
html-b07-paragraphs.why: pre switches off whitespace collapsing and renders in a monospaced font, so typed spaces and line breaks reach the screen exactly as written.

html-b08-text-formatting.q: A safety notice must convey 'do not skip this' to every reader, including screen-reader users. Which element carries that meaning?
options: <b>, because bold draws the eye
<strong>, which marks serious importance rather than just bold styling
<mark>, because highlighting is stronger than bold
<u>, because underlines signal importance
html-b08-text-formatting.why: strong states importance semantically — assistive technology can convey it, and machines reading the page treat the content as genuinely important. b is visual offset only.

html-b08-text-formatting.q: You are marking up 'She boarded the Aurora' where Aurora is a ship's name conventionally set in italics, with no extra stress. Which element fits?
options: <em>, because it renders italic
<i>, which marks conventional italics without claiming emphasis
<cite>, because ships are creative works
<q>, because names are quotations
html-b08-text-formatting.why: i is for typographic-convention italics: ship names, foreign phrases, technical terms. em would falsely add spoken stress, and cite is for titles of works.

html-b08-text-formatting.q: A product listing must show the price changed from $50 to $40, keeping the old price visible. Which markup records the change semantically?
options: <del>$50</del> <ins>$40</ins>
<small>$50</small> <mark>$40</mark>
html-b08-text-formatting.why: del marks removed content and ins marks its replacement — an explicit edit record that assistive technology can announce, unlike purely visual strikethrough.

html-b09-quotations.q: You quote a full paragraph from a public speech and want to record the transcript's URL machine-readably. Which markup is correct?
options: ...
<q href="https://example.com/transcript">...</q>
<cite src="https://example.com/transcript">...</cite>
...
html-b09-quotations.why: Block-level quotations take blockquote, whose optional cite attribute holds the source URL as invisible metadata. q is for inline quotes and cite (the element) marks visible work titles.

html-b09-quotations.q: Marking up an inline quote with <q>, a colleague also types quotation marks around the words. What happens?
options: Nothing — the browser removes the duplicates
The marks display doubled, because the browser generates q's quotation marks automatically
The page fails validation and will not render
The typed marks override the automatic ones
html-b09-quotations.why: q supplies language-appropriate quotation marks itself — hand-typed ones stack on top of them. Write the quoted words bare inside q.

html-b09-quotations.q: An article says 'Published on 5 March 2026' and you want search engines to parse the date reliably. What do you add?
options: <date value="05-03-2026"> around the text
<time datetime="2026-03-05"> around the human-readable date
<meta date="March 5"> in the paragraph
Nothing — search engines always parse written dates correctly
html-b09-quotations.why: The time element pairs human text with an unambiguous ISO value (year-month-day) in its datetime attribute — the standard way to make dates machine-readable.

html-b10-comments.q: You need to hide an unfinished section before a demo but restore it next week. What is the standard approach?
options: Delete the markup and retype it later
Wrap the section in <!-- and --> so it stays in the file but never renders
Set every element's font size to zero
Move the markup into the head element
html-b10-comments.why: Commenting-out disables markup without losing it — the parser skips comment contents entirely, and restoring the section means deleting two markers.

html-b10-comments.q: A developer leaves <!-- staging server: admin.internal.example.com, password Winter26 --> in a page. What is the risk?
options: None — comments never leave the developer's machine
The comment slows down page rendering
Every visitor can read it via view-source; comments ship publicly with the page
Browsers may execute the comment as code
html-b10-comments.why: Comments are invisible in the rendered page but fully present in the delivered HTML. Credentials and internal details in comments are a real, commonly exploited leak.

html-b10-comments.q: You wrap an already-commented block inside another comment and suddenly raw markup appears on the page. Why?
options: Comments cannot contain the letter sequence 'TODO'
Comments do not nest: the outer comment ends at the first -->, exposing everything after it
The browser ran out of comment memory
Two comments on one page is the maximum
html-b10-comments.why: The parser closes a comment at the first --> it encounters, so the inner comment's closing marker terminates the outer one and the remainder renders as content.

html-b11-links.q: From your site's resources page you link to another organisation's documentation site. Which href form is required?
options: docs.html — relative paths reach any site
../external/docs — climbing out of your site's folder
https://docs.example.org/guide — an absolute URL with scheme and domain
#docs.example.org — a fragment reference
html-b11-links.why: Leaving your own site requires the complete address: scheme plus domain. Relative paths only resolve within the current site's structure.

html-b11-links.q: A screen-reader user pulls up the list of links on your page and hears 'click here' five times. What was the authoring mistake?
options: Too many links on one page
Link text that only works in surrounding context — links should name their destination
Missing target attributes on the links
The links were not underlined
html-b11-links.why: Links are often read out of context — in link lists and by scanning — so each link's own text must identify where it leads. 'Click here' identifies nothing.

html-b11-links.q: You wrap your site logo in a link to the home page. What should the img's alt text say?
options: A visual description of the artwork, like 'blue hexagon'
Nothing — linked images should have empty alt text
The link's destination, like 'ExampleCo home', since the alt becomes the link's accessible name
The word 'image' so users know it is a picture
html-b11-links.why: For a linked image the alt text names the link, not the picture. Empty alt would leave the link with no announced name at all — a common accessibility failure.

html-b12-file-paths.q: The page articles/first-post.html must show images/logo.png, where images/ sits at the project root. Which src is correct?
options: images/logo.png
../images/logo.png
/articles/images/logo.png
..images/logo.png
html-b12-file-paths.why: Relative paths start from the containing file: from inside articles/, one ../ climbs to the root, then images/logo.png descends to the file.

html-b12-file-paths.q: Your navigation uses href="/contact.html" and works perfectly on the deployed site, but every nav link 404s when you open the files from disk. Why?
options: Root-relative paths resolve against a web server's site root, which does not exist when browsing via file://
Browsers block navigation between local files
The leading slash is a typo that servers silently fix
contact.html must be renamed index.html first
html-b12-file-paths.why: A leading / anchors the path to the site root that a server defines. Opened from disk, it points at the drive's root instead — so use relative paths while testing local files.

html-b12-file-paths.q: Visitors should reach your site's front page at https://example.com/ with no filename in the URL. What makes that work?
options: Registering the domain with a homepage certificate
Naming the front page index.html — the default file servers serve for a folder request
Adding a homepage attribute to the html element
Creating a file literally named example.com
html-b12-file-paths.why: When a URL requests a folder, the server looks for the conventional default file, index.html, and serves it — the convention behind every clean homepage URL.
